messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Vignette:
Minh Tran was 46 when he first came to treatment, a divorced firefighter who had spent a period working as a relief responder in a war zone overseas, an assignment he had taken on with the assumption that he could do practical good in a place that had been devastated by violence. He spoke quietly about that time, but the details came in fragments, as though he had to reach around them rather than toward them. He described streets that had gone suddenly still except for the sharp, tearing sound of explosions, and he said that even now a bang in the distance could make his whole body go rigid before he had time to think. During the deployment he had been around scenes of chaos and human suffering that he found difficult to put into any orderly sequence afterward; when he tried to tell others about it, he would sometimes stop in the middle of a sentence because the right words would not come. What he knew happened was clear to him, yet the memories did not stay arranged in the order he wanted, and that disjointedness had become part of how he experienced those events.

There was one stretch of the deployment he returned to again and again, though never in a complete way. He remembered being confronted with behavior that felt morally wrong to him, moments in which people around him were acting with callousness or abuse while others were vulnerable. He did not elaborate easily, but his face tightened when he spoke about misbehavior and about comments he had heard later regarding sexual violence. Those remarks, especially when spoken casually, seemed to pull him back into the same sense of contamination and disgust he had felt in the war zone. He said it was not only the memory of what he saw but the feeling that something in him had been crossed as well. He had come to believe that he acted in ways that went against who he was, and that belief sat heavily with him. He talked about the deployment as the point after which his life had been “broken in half,” saying flatly that his life had been destroyed by the trauma and that he no longer belonged anywhere.

Over time, Minh began to notice that certain moments in daily life pulled the war back into the present with disturbing force. In the firehouse, if someone made a cutting joke about sexual violence or repeated a crude story, he would feel the familiar jolt of alarm and moral revulsion, often needing to leave the room without explanation. He also found himself scanning for signs that something bad was about to happen whenever there was unusual silence around him. The quiet in a station kitchen, a pause in conversation after a radio transmission, or an unexpectedly still stretch during a shift could make him feel that danger was close, as if silence itself were a warning. On other days, it was sound that did it: a slammed metal door, a construction blast nearby, or an explosion-like bang could flood his body with the same shock he remembered from overseas. He described becoming irritable with coworkers and family, snapping in anger over small frustrations, then feeling ashamed afterward. The anger sometimes felt so hard to hold that he would clamp down on his reactions at work and then release them later at home, where the consequences were harder to hide.

Minh coped in ways that he knew were not helping but that made sense to him in the moment. He tried hard not to think about the deployment, pushing away images when they appeared, but they still came back. At times, when the memories became overwhelming, he hurt himself physically to release the feeling, saying that pain he could choose felt easier than the pressure building inside him. He also performed mental rituals, silently repeating thoughts in a fixed sequence in hopes of preventing bad things from happening again. He knew the rituals did not really make him safe, but he felt compelled to do them anyway, especially after a loud noise or a moment of silence that seemed ominous. When the memory returned, he noticed a strange bodily echo of the event: pain in the same parts of his body where he had felt strain and injury during the war zone work. That physical return of pain made the memories feel less like thoughts than like events happening again in his body.

At home, the pattern had narrowed his world. After his divorce, he found it increasingly difficult to feel that he had a place with anyone, and he carried that sense of not belonging into friendships, family gatherings, and even the station culture he had once relied on. He continued to work as a firefighter, but the job now brought repeated exposure to the sounds and silences that unsettled him, and he had become wary of group settings where crude remarks could surface without warning. What finally brought him in was the sense that he was no longer able to keep the whole thing contained. He was frightened by how often he was angry, by the moments when he hurt himself to get through a wave of feeling, and by the possibility that one sudden bang or one more stretch of silence might send him back into the worst of it. More than anything, Minh hoped for relief from the constant sense that something dangerous was about to happen and for some way to live without feeling that he had permanently lost both his place in the world and his own sense of who he was.
